title: One case study, all semester
text: Every week builds on the same Online Shop database: customers, products, suppliers, orders, order items and inventory. You start with the normalised design in Week 1 and keep adding to it, so by Week 12 you have seen every technique the assessment asks for working together in one system. Your own assessed project uses a business scenario you choose; the Online Shop is the worked example you learn from. How the Online Shop grows across the module Four stages: database design (weeks 1 to 3), application (weeks 4 and 5), security and data (weeks 6 to 10), and integration (weeks 11 and 12). Weeks 1–3 · Database 3NF schema & ERD Triggers Views, functions, optimised queries Weeks 4–5 · Application

title: Run this site locally
text: The site is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step. The SQL playgrounds load a WebAssembly build of SQLite and a database file, and browsers only allow that over http:// . Double-clicking index.html opens it as file:// instead, so start a small local web server: py -m http.server 8000 Then open http://localhost:8000/ . Press Ctrl + C in the terminal to stop the server. Everything the site needs is included locally, so it works without an internet connection, which is useful in classrooms with unreliable Wi-Fi.

title: Learning outcomes
text: By the end of this week you should be able to: Distinguish data from information and explain what a database management system does. Compare relational and NoSQL databases and say when each is appropriate. Identify primary, candidate, composite, surrogate and foreign keys and the integrity rules they enforce. Identify functional dependencies and explain update, insertion and deletion anomalies . Normalise a flat file from UNF to 3NF, justifying each step. Draw and read ER diagrams in Crow’s Foot and Chen notation, including cardinality and participation. Map an ER diagram to SQLite tables with appropriate integrity constraints, and query it from Python.

title: Why this matters
text: Most business data starts life in a spreadsheet. A small online shop might keep one sheet with a row per order: the customer’s name, address and phone, then each product, its price and supplier. It works until the shop grows. A customer moves house and the address is updated in one row but not in the other twelve, so a parcel goes to the wrong address. A product is discontinued, the rows that mention it are deleted, and the only record of its supplier goes with them. A data-protection request asks for everything held about one person, and it is scattered across hundreds of rows. Normalisation is the systematic way to remove these problems before they happen, and an ER diagram is how database

title: Relational and NoSQL databases
text: The relational model was proposed by E. F. Codd at IBM in 1970. A relational database stores data in tables (relations) with a fixed schema. Tables are linked by key values and queried with SQL. Relational databases give strong integrity guarantees and ACID transactions (atomic, consistent, isolated, durable): ideal when many related rows must change together correctly, such as an order and its stock update. NoSQL (“not only SQL”) is a family of non-relational databases designed for flexible or changing structure, very large scale, or particular data shapes. Amazon’s Dynamo and Google’s Bigtable papers inspired many of them. The four main families: The four NoSQL data models Document { "orde

text: Formal term Everyday term Online Shop example Relation Table customer Tuple Row / record Jane Morris’s row Attribute Column / field email Domain Allowed values for a column status ∈ {Pending, Paid, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled} Degree Number of columns customer has degree 8 Cardinality (of a table) Number of rows customer has cardinality 8 (not the same as ER cardinality, below)

title: Keys
text: Super key Any set of columns whose values are unique for every row, e.g. (customer_id, email) . Candidate key A minimal super key: remove any column and it stops being unique. customer_id and email are both candidate keys of customer . Primary key (PK) The candidate key chosen to identify rows. Must be unique and never NULL. customer.customer_id . Alternate key A candidate key not chosen as the PK. Enforce it with UNIQUE ( customer.email ). Composite key A key made of two or more columns: order_item (order_id, product_id) . Natural vs surrogate A natural key has real-world meaning (an e-mail, a car registration). A surrogate key is a meaningless number generated by the database ( customer_id

title: Integrity rules
text: Entity integrity : every row has a primary key value that is unique and not NULL. Referential integrity : every foreign key value matches an existing key in the referenced table (or is NULL, if allowed). Domain integrity : values are of the right kind and within allowed limits ( NOT NULL , CHECK (price >= 0) , DEFAULT ). Two SQLite surprises 1. Foreign keys are off by default. Every new connection must run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; or SQLite silently ignores every REFERENCES clause. 2. Non-integer primary keys can be NULL unless you also write NOT NULL (a historical quirk). INTEGER PRIMARY KEY columns are safe: they are the table’s row id and are filled in automatically.

title: The parts of SQL
text: Sub-language Purpose Statements In SQLite DDL: Data Definition Define structure CREATE , ALTER , DROP Yes DML: Data Manipulation Read and change rows SELECT , INSERT , UPDATE , DELETE (some books list SELECT separately as DQL , Data Query Language) Yes DCL: Data Control Control who may access data GRANT , REVOKE No: use file permissions TCL: Transaction Control Group changes into transactions BEGIN , COMMIT , ROLLBACK , SAVEPOINT Yes (Week 11) Some commands in general SQL cheat-sheets are not in SQLite: there is no TRUNCATE (use DELETE FROM table; ) and no MERGE (use INSERT … ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE , an “upsert”).

title: Why normalise? Data anomalies
text: Redundancy means storing the same fact more than once. It wastes space, but the real damage is that the copies can drift apart. In a single “everything in one table” design, redundancy causes three kinds of anomaly . The table below is the shop’s order spreadsheet after the first clean-up step (1NF), with one row per product in an order. Try each anomaly: Anomaly What goes wrong Root cause Update Changing one fact means changing many rows; miss one and the data contradicts itself. The same fact is stored in several rows. Insertion You cannot record one fact without inventing another (a product without an order). Unrelated facts share a primary key. Deletion Deleting one fact accidentally des

title: Functional dependencies
text: Attribute Y is functionally dependent on attribute(s) X , written X → Y , if each value of X is always associated with exactly one value of Y . X is called the determinant . email → phone : knowing a customer’s e-mail tells you their (single) phone number. product → price : each product has one price. (order_no, product) → qty : you need both to know how many were ordered. product → qty does not hold: the same product is ordered in different quantities. Dependencies come from business rules, not from sample data Five rows can disprove a dependency (two rows with the same X but different Y) but can never prove one. In the fruit-shop data four customers share one phone number, so phone → custo

title: Three kinds of dependency
text: When the primary key is (order_no, product) : full A non-key attribute depends on the whole key: (order_no, product) → qty . This is what we want. partial A non-key attribute depends on part of a composite key: order_no → order_date . Breaks 2NF . transitive A non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute: supplier → supplier_phone (key → product → supplier → supplier_phone). Breaks 3NF . Try it: classify each dependency (primary key = order_no + product) (order_no, product) → qty order_no → order_date product → price email → phone supplier → supplier_phone order_no → email category → vat_rate postcode → county Reset

title: Normalising step by step: UNF → 3NF
text: Form Rule How to get there UNF Unnormalised: cells may hold several values, groups of values repeat, no key. — 1NF Every cell holds a single (atomic) value; no repeating groups; each row identified by a primary key. Split multi-part values into columns; give each repeated item its own row; choose a key. 2NF 1NF, and no partial dependency: every non-key attribute depends on the whole key. Move attributes that depend on part of the key into a new table with that part as its key. 3NF 2NF, and no transitive dependency: no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute. Move the dependent attributes into a new table keyed by their determinant; leave a foreign key behind. Memory aid In 3NF

title: Beyond 3NF, and when to denormalise
text: There are more normal forms than three. Each removes a rarer kind of redundancy: Form Removes Example BCNF (Boyce–Codd) Any dependency whose determinant is not a candidate key (student, module) → tutor where each tutor teaches only one module ( tutor → module ). This is 3NF but not BCNF. 4NF Independent multi-valued facts stored together A table of (employee, skill, language): skills and languages are unrelated lists. 5NF Join dependencies (data that can only be rebuilt from three or more projections) Rare in practice. 6NF, DKNF Theoretical forms used in specialist (e.g. temporal) databases — For most business systems 3NF (or BCNF) is the practical target , and 3NF is what the assessment ask

title: ER modelling concepts
text: An entity–relationship (ER) model describes the things a business needs to keep data about and how they relate. It is drawn as an ER diagram (ERD) before any SQL is written. Entity A thing of interest with its own identity: CUSTOMER, PRODUCT, ORDERS. (An entity type is the category; an instance is one occurrence, such as Jane.) Attribute A property of an entity. It can be simple or composite (an address made of street and postcode), single- or multi-valued (several phone numbers), and stored or derived (order total = Σ quantity × unit price). Key attribute An attribute that uniquely identifies each instance. Relationship An association between entities: a customer places orders. Its degree i

title: A unary (recursive) relationship
text: In a unary relationship an entity is related to itself , playing two roles . The classic example comes from the original Week 1 database: the EMP table, where each employee’s mgr column holds the empno of their manager. Each employee (as a manager) manages zero or many employees; each employee (as a subordinate) is managed by zero or one employee, since the president has none. In tables it is simply a foreign key that references the same table , and you query it by joining the table to itself with two aliases:

title: Cardinality and participation
text: Each end of a relationship has two numbers: Maximum (cardinality) : one or many . This gives the relationship type: 1:1, 1:N or M:N. Minimum (participation / optionality) : zero (optional, partial participation) or one (mandatory, total participation). Read a relationship in both directions , starting each sentence with “Each”: Reading CUSTOMER — places — ORDERS Each customer places zero or many orders (a new customer may not have ordered yet). Each order is placed by exactly one customer (an order cannot exist without its customer). Cardinalities come from business rules . Write the rule first, then draw the symbols: Business rule (Online Shop) Min Max A customer may have an online account,

title: Crow’s Foot and Chen notation
text: Both notations describe the same model. Chen (Peter Chen, 1976) is conceptual : it shows entities, attributes and relationships without implementation detail. Crow’s Foot (also called Information Engineering notation) is usually logical : boxes look like tables and list keys and foreign keys. It is the default in tools such as MySQL Workbench, Lucidchart and draw.io. This module uses Crow’s Foot by default ; you should be able to read both. Element Crow’s Foot Chen Entity Box with the name in a header Rectangle Attributes Listed inside the box, often with data types Ovals connected to the entity Primary key Marked PK (and often underlined) Attribute name underlined Foreign key Shown and mark

title: One-to-one (1:1)
text: Each customer has zero or one account; each account belongs to exactly one customer. Toggle the notation to compare: the optional side becomes a circle in Crow’s Foot and a single line in Chen. The Crow’s Foot line is dashed because the relationship is non-identifying : account_id , not customer_id , identifies an account.

title: One-to-many (1:N)
text: The most common relationship. Each customer places zero or many orders; each order is placed by exactly one customer. In Chen, ORDERS has a double line (total participation) because every order must have a customer.

title: Many-to-many (M:N)
text: An order contains one or many products; a product appears in zero or many orders. Chen draws this directly, and the relationship owns attributes (quantity, unit price) that belong to neither entity alone.

title: Why INVENTORY is a weak entity in the Chen diagram
text: A weak entity has no key of its own: it is identified through its owner . An inventory record means nothing without the product it counts, and the database identifies it by the product’s key ( inventory.product_id is the whole primary key). In Chen notation this is shown three ways: INVENTORY is a double rectangle (weak entity); HAS_STOCK is a double diamond (the identifying relationship that supplies the key); INVENTORY has a double line to HAS_STOCK, because a weak entity always has total participation in its identifying relationship. The cardinality is 1:1, so INVENTORY needs no partial key (the dashed-underlined discriminator that a weak entity has when one owner can have several, such a

title: From conceptual (Chen) to logical (Crow’s Foot)
text: The two diagrams above are the same design at two levels . Chen records what the business needs; Crow’s Foot records how it is stored in tables. Moving from one to the other is a set of mechanical rules: In the Chen (conceptual) model Becomes in the Crow’s Foot (logical) model Entity CUSTOMER with key attribute customer_id Table customer , customer_id PK 1:N relationship PLACES (ORDERS total) FK orders.customer_id on the N side, NOT NULL because ORDERS participates totally; drawn as a dashed (non-identifying) line 1:1 relationship HAS (USER_ACCOUNT total, CUSTOMER partial) FK user_account.customer_id on the side that participates totally, made UNIQUE to keep it 1:1 M:N relationship CONTAINS

title: Mapping an ER diagram to tables
text: Each strong entity becomes a table. Simple attributes become columns; the key becomes the PRIMARY KEY . Composite attributes are split into their parts ( address_line , postcode ). Multi-valued attributes move to their own table, e.g. customer_phone(customer_id, phone) if a customer could have several numbers. 1:N : put a foreign key in the table on the many side ( orders.customer_id ). Make it NOT NULL when participation on that side is total. 1:1 : put the foreign key on the optional or dependent side and add UNIQUE ( user_account.customer_id ). Without UNIQUE it would be 1:N. M:N : create a junction table holding both foreign keys, usually as a composite primary key. The relationship’s at

title: Connecting from Python
text: The same database is used from Python with the built-in sqlite3 module. That is the foundation of the Tkinter application from Week 4. The full script is explore_shop_v1.py ; here are the key parts, step by step.

title: 1. Connect, and switch foreign keys on
text: import sqlite3 from pathlib import Path # Find the database next to THIS script, wherever the folder is. DB_PATH = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "shop_v1.db" def connect(path=DB_PATH): con = sqlite3.connect(path) con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row # access columns by name: row["email"] con.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON") # OFF by default, on EVERY connection return con Path(__file__).resolve().parent replaces hard-coded paths such as C:\Users\Admin\Downloads\db1.db , which break on every other computer, including the marker’s.

title: Common mistakes and debugging
text: Mistake Why it is wrong Fix Lists in a cell: "COM10, COM67" Not atomic, so not even 1NF. You cannot query or join on it. One row per value, in a separate table. Name or phone as primary key Not unique: four fruit-shop customers share a phone number. A surrogate INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , plus UNIQUE on true candidate keys. Splitting tables but losing the link A “lossy” decomposition: you can no longer tell which products were in which order. Keep the key columns (and FKs) needed to join back; test with a JOIN. One “quantity” column for two meanings Quantity ordered belongs to the order line; quantity in stock belongs to the product. Name columns precisely: quantity , qty_in_stock . M:N relationsh

title: Reading SQLite error messages
text: Message Meaning FOREIGN KEY constraint failed The referenced row does not exist, or you tried to delete a parent that still has children (RESTRICT). UNIQUE constraint failed: customer.email That value already exists in a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY column. NOT NULL constraint failed: product.name A required column was left empty. CHECK constraint failed: quantity > 0 The value broke a CHECK rule. near "order": syntax error You used a reserved word as a table name. Rename it to orders . no such table: customer You are connected to a different (often brand-new, empty) database file. Check the path.

title: Summary and next steps
text: Data becomes information through processing; a DBMS stores data and protects its integrity. Relational databases suit structured, related data that needs transactions; NoSQL suits huge, flexible or graph-shaped data. Redundancy causes update, insertion and deletion anomalies. Normalisation stores each fact once. 1NF: atomic values and a key. 2NF: no partial dependencies. 3NF: no transitive dependencies. ER diagrams show entities, attributes and relationships, each with a cardinality and participation. Crow’s Foot is logical and shows keys; Chen is conceptual and shows relationships as diamonds. Mapping: 1:N → FK on the many side; 1:1 → FK + UNIQUE; M:N → junction table. In SQLite always run

title: Why this matters
text: Last week the Online Shop database learned to reject impossible data: an order for a customer who does not exist, a negative price. It still accepts plenty of data that is possible but wrong for the business . A customer can order 10 cheddars when 4 are in stock. A delivered order can be quietly edited. Stock levels drift away from what was actually sold. Nobody can say who changed a price, or when. Real systems handle these rules with triggers : small programs stored inside the database that run automatically whenever data changes. Because they live in the database, they apply to every program that touches the data: the Tkinter app you build in Week 4, an import script, or someone typing SQ

title: Before you start
text: You need the Week 1 schema (customer, product, inventory, orders, order_item…), and to be comfortable with UPDATE … SET … WHERE and with a subquery that returns one value, such as (SELECT qty_in_stock FROM inventory WHERE product_id = 9) .

title: What is a trigger?
text: A trigger is a named block of SQL that the database runs automatically when a specified change happens to a specified table. You never call a trigger yourself: the database fires it. Every trigger follows the event → condition → action (ECA) pattern: Part Question it answers Online Shop example Event Which change on which table? INSERT ON order_item Timing Before or after the row is changed (or instead of it)? AFTER Condition (optional) Should it run for this row? WHEN NEW.quantity > 0 Action What SQL runs? UPDATE inventory SET qty_in_stock = qty_in_stock - NEW.quantity … Benefits Rules live in one place. Every program that changes the data obeys them; you do not re-code them in each applica

title: Trigger syntax in SQLite
text: CREATE [TEMP] TRIGGER [IF NOT EXISTS] trigger_name { BEFORE | AFTER | INSTEAD OF } { INSERT | UPDATE [OF column, …] | DELETE } ON table_or_view_name [FOR EACH ROW] [WHEN condition] BEGIN statement; -- INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or SELECT statement; -- as many as you need, each ending with ; END; trigger_name Must be unique in the database. A naming convention such as trg_table_purpose makes triggers easy to find. BEFORE / AFTER Whether the action runs before or after the row is changed. On tables only. INSTEAD OF Replaces the change entirely. On views only (see below). UPDATE OF col, … Fire only when one of these columns appears in the SET list of the UPDATE. FOR EACH ROW The trigger runs once p

title: Managing triggers
text: -- List every trigger, with the table it belongs to SELECT name, tbl_name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'trigger' ORDER BY tbl_name, name; -- Show the full definition of one trigger SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'trigger' AND name = 'trg_order_item_sale'; There is no ALTER TRIGGER in SQLite: to change a trigger, DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS name; and create it again. Dropping a table also drops its triggers. In DB Browser for SQLite, triggers appear under Database Structure → Triggers .

title: OLD and NEW
text: Inside a trigger, NEW and OLD refer to the row being changed. Which ones exist depends on the event: Event OLD.column NEW.column Typical use INSERT ✗ (no old row) ✓ the row being added Check or react to the new data UPDATE ✓ values before the change ✓ values after the change Compare: what changed, by how much? DELETE ✓ the row being removed ✗ (no new row) Undo its effects; archive it A mistake SQLite does not catch until it runs A trigger that uses NEW in a DELETE trigger (or OLD in an INSERT trigger) is created without any error . It only fails when it fires, with no such column: NEW.quantity . Always test every trigger by actually firing it.

title: Your first trigger: logging new customers
text: The original Week 2 example logged every new employee into emp_log . Here is the same idea for the shop: whenever a customer registers, an AFTER INSERT trigger writes a row to a log table using NEW . Run it, then change the INSERT and run it again. NEW.customer_id already holds the id SQLite generated, because an AFTER trigger runs once the row exists.

title: BEFORE, AFTER and INSTEAD OF: the execution flow
text: What exactly happens when one statement fires triggers? For each row the statement touches, SQLite runs the steps below in order. This flow is the most useful thing to understand when a trigger does something unexpected. How SQLite runs a statement that fires triggers For each affected row: BEFORE triggers, then constraint checks and the row change, then AFTER triggers, which may fire further triggers. At the end of the statement foreign keys are checked. A RAISE or a constraint failure at any step undoes the statement. INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE statement for EACH affected row ① BEFORE triggers run if their WHEN is true · use for validation ② Constraints checked, row written NOT NULL · CHECK

title: Step 1: the problem
text: Adding 5 × Basmati Rice to an order should reduce the stock of rice from 70 to 65. Does it?

title: Step 2: a first attempt, and why it is wrong
text: The original slides’ first attempt set the stock to a fixed number. It changes the data, but it is wrong for every order except one:

title: Step 3: use NEW
text: NEW holds the row just inserted, so the trigger can use its quantity and its product:

title: Step 4: what if there is not enough stock?
text: Only 4 Cheddar are in stock. With the Step 3 trigger, ordering 10 would make the stock −6. Our Week 1 schema already has CHECK (qty_in_stock >= 0) , so the AFTER trigger’s UPDATE fails and the whole INSERT is undone. That is defence in depth , but the error ( CHECK constraint failed ) means nothing to a shop assistant. A BEFORE trigger can refuse the order earlier, with a clear message. The original slides gave two solutions: Solution 1: CASE inside the body CREATE TRIGGER trg_check_stock_v1 BEFORE INSERT ON order_item BEGIN SELECT CASE WHEN (SELECT qty_in_stock FROM inventory WHERE product_id = NEW.product_id) < NEW.quantity THEN RAISE(ABORT, 'Not enough stock') END; END; Solution 2: a WHEN

title: Writing good WHEN conditions
text: Fire only on real changes. UPDATE OF price fires whenever price appears in the SET list, even if the value is the same . Add WHEN NEW.price <> OLD.price . Compare NULL-safely. OLD.phone <> NEW.phone is NULL when either is NULL, so a change to or from NULL would be missed. Use OLD.phone IS NOT NEW.phone . Detect crossings, not states. A reorder alert should be raised when stock falls to the reorder level, not on every later sale: WHEN NEW.qty_in_stock <= NEW.reorder_level AND OLD.qty_in_stock > OLD.reorder_level .

title: RAISE() options
text: RAISE() can only be used inside a trigger. Its message must be a plain string literal, such as 'Not enough stock' ; it cannot be built from NEW values in the SQLite versions used in this module. Form Effect In Python RAISE(ABORT, 'msg') Stops the statement and undoes all of its changes , including those made by triggers. Earlier statements in the same transaction are kept. The usual choice. sqlite3.IntegrityError: msg RAISE(FAIL, 'msg') Stops the statement but keeps rows it had already changed (e.g. the first rows of a multi-row INSERT). IntegrityError RAISE(ROLLBACK, 'msg') Rolls back the whole transaction , not just this statement. IntegrityError , transaction ended RAISE(IGNORE) Silently

title: Audit logging
text: An audit trail records who changed what, when, from what and to what. Triggers are ideal for this because they cannot be bypassed by forgetting to call a logging function. What to record: the table and key of the changed row, the action, the old and new values, and a timestamp ( datetime('now') is UTC). No foreign keys on audit tables. A log must keep its rows even after the audited row is deleted, so audit_log has none. Who made the change? SQLite has no user accounts, so it has no CURRENT_USER . The application must record the user, for example by writing to an changed_by column. Client–server databases can log the database user automatically. Personal data. Audit logs of customer details

title: Cascading, recursion and firing order
text: Cascading triggers A trigger’s action can fire other triggers, as when a sale updates inventory, which raises a reorder alert. SQLite allows this, up to a depth limit of 1000. Recursive triggers A trigger that (directly or indirectly) fires itself , e.g. an AFTER UPDATE on inventory that updates inventory. SQLite blocks this by default ( PRAGMA recursive_triggers is OFF). Do not turn it on unless you are sure the recursion stops. Foreign-key actions fire triggers ON DELETE CASCADE deletes child rows as if by a DELETE statement, so their DELETE triggers run. Deleting a pending order in shop_v2 therefore returns its stock through trg_order_item_removed . Several triggers on one event The order

title: INSTEAD OF triggers on views
text: A view is a stored query that behaves like a read-only table (Week 3 covers views in depth). You cannot INSERT into a view directly, because it has no rows of its own. An INSTEAD OF trigger tells SQLite what to do instead , usually by changing the underlying tables. Fire it with one row and look at every table it should change, before and after (just like the trigger lab). Add a temporary log: INSERT INTO debug_log VALUES ('reached step 2', NEW.quantity); inside the body, then remove it. Check for other triggers on the same table that might interfere: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='trigger' AND tbl_name='order_item'; Mistake Symptom Fix Fixed values in the body ( SET qty_in_stock = 99 WHERE product_id = 9 ) Works for one test,

title: Summary and next steps
text: A trigger is event → (condition) → action, fired automatically for each row . BEFORE validates and refuses with RAISE ; AFTER carries out consequences in other tables; INSTEAD OF makes views updatable. INSERT has NEW , DELETE has OLD , UPDATE has both. Use UPDATE OF and WHEN so a trigger only fires when it should. RAISE(ABORT) undoes everything the statement did, including other triggers’ work, and arrives in Python as IntegrityError . SQLite triggers are row-level only, cannot assign NEW , have plain-SQL bodies and fire in an unguaranteed order. Audit tables record old and new values and have no foreign keys. text: The original Task 1 asked for an order_cost table maintained by triggers. Build order_total(order_id, total) and keep it correct whenever an order line is inserted, updated or deleted. title: Glossary
text: Audit trail An append-only record of changes: what, when, old and new values. Cascading trigger A trigger fired by another trigger’s action. ECA Event → condition → action: the structure of every trigger. INSTEAD OF A trigger that replaces an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a view. NEW / OLD The row after / before the change, inside a row-level trigger. RAISE() Stops or skips the current change from inside a trigger (ABORT, FAIL, ROLLBACK, IGNORE). Recursive trigger A trigger that fires itself. Off by default in SQLite. Row-level trigger Runs once for every row a statement affects (the only kind in SQLite).
